views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold our current tariff threat as leverage but do not escalate further, and actively pursue a negotiated settlement on intellectual property and technology-transfer practices. The proposed $50B Section 301 duties should remain on the table as a bargaining chip, but we should use the long implementation runway (public hearing May 15, comments to May 22, ~180 days after) to press Beijing for concrete structural concessions rather than piling on additional tariffs. Avoid escalating toward the further $100B in duties that has been floated, which would inflame domestic farm-state backlash and market jitters with little added negotiating leverage.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is moderate but real — roughly +0.3, not existential. The dispute is US-initiated and the US economy remains strong (industrial production 103.3 and rising, consumer sentiment ~98.8, CPI ~1.2%, 10-yr at 2.79% with no trade-war damage yet in the macro data), while the trade asymmetry favors us: our $50B in proposed tariffs is a small share of Chinese imports whereas China's matching retaliation is a far larger relative share of US exports, giving us room to sustain pressure (NYT asymmetry note, Apr 4). However, China deliberately aimed its retaliation at politically sensitive US agriculture — soybeans, corn, wheat, pork — hitting Trump's farm-belt base ahead of the 2018 midterms; soybean futures fell ~5% and the American Soybean Association publicly decried a 'devastating' effect and called on the White House to reconsider (CNBC/FoodNavigator, Apr 4-6). That is real domestic political exposure that argues against reflexively escalating. At the same time, markets largely de-rated the tit-for-tat as 'negotiating theater' and both sides publicly disavowed a full trade war ('we are not in a trade war with China'; Kudlow stressing 'delicate negotiations'). Because we retain strong leverage but face genuine domestic political cost from further escalation, the disciplined stance is to negotiate — keeping the tariff threat as the stick to win structural IP/tech-transfer reforms while de-escalating on the most politically explosive front. Escalation would make it worse for us at home before the midterms; concession would throw away our leverage.
key_factors: US initiated escalation with strong leverage (tariff asymmetry favors US; $50B is small vs. Chinese imports but China's is large vs. US exports)
US macro is strong — no real-economy damage yet (IP 103.3 rising, sentiment ~98.8, CPI ~1.2%)
China's retaliation targeted politically sensitive US farm-belt exports (soybeans, corn, wheat, pork) and Boeing ahead of 2018 midterms
Soybean futures fell ~5%, farm groups (ASA) publicly urging de-escalation — mounting domestic political pressure
Nothing in effect yet: long runway (hearing May 15, comments to May 22, ~180 days) enables negotiation
Markets treating moves as negotiating theater; both sides publicly disavow a full trade war
Further escalation ($100B more) risks farm backlash + market jitters without added leverage

sources_cited.excerpt: USTR Section 301 report finds China's IP/tech-transfer practices unreasonable; Trump directs tariffs, WTO case, investment restrictions
USTR publishes proposed Section 301 tariff list: ~1,300 Chinese product lines (~$50B); public comment opens
China announces proposed retaliatory tariffs on ~$50B of US goods (soybeans, autos, aircraft)
US industrial production 103.3 (Apr 2018), rising — no trade-war damage yet
China targets US soybean trade (~$14B; buys ~half of US soybean exports); soybean futures fell ~5%; ASA calls it 'devastating'
US imports far more from China, giving US more room to target Chinese goods; retaliatory duties hit farm belt/Republican states
Dow rebounded ~230 pts; investors view moves as 'negotiating theater'; Kudlow: 'delicate negotiations'; Trump: 'not in a trade war'
Trump orders USTR to consider $100B in additional Section 301 tariffs — further escalation option
